Hi, Esther Sammer. I live in Tarrytown. As a member of the Field Committee, I'd like to express my appreciation for the opportunity to serve it. There was a lot of common ground in the committee. For example, we agreed on a natural turf field for Eastfield. We agreed that the condition of Mazzaro's field is extremely poor. We agreed that our four fields are interdependent and that we all support our athletic program and we all value our fields. There were differences of opinion, though, about how to achieve our goals. Some members of the committee were committed to explore explore whether natural turf was a viable option for Mazzaro's field for both environmental and cost reasons. Understanding the way the field is actually used was of prime importance. You can't just take the number of hours that our sports teams play, add youth recreation, sports, and PE, divide that by the number of available fields and come up with a number. Raw data needs to be synthesized before understanding can be reached. For example, when sports turf managers say that a natural turf field can be used for 700 hours, they're talking about 700 hours of professional athletic play, the hardest use. PE is negligible use in comparison, which is why it is typically not used in such a calculation. Raw data might include PE hours, which accounts for half of the stated use for Mazzaro's field, but synthesized data really should not. those hours away and we are under 700 hours of use from Mazzaro's field. There are other examples of the difference between raw and synthesized data that I could mention but it won't because of time. When we see a photograph of Mazzaro's field after heavy snow melt and rain, we see a field that has not been restored in over 20 years, that has compacted soil, poor drainage, and is, to use a dramatic metaphor, in cardiac arrest. This isn't the result of natural grass. If we took a photograph of a memorial field the day after rain, it would look beautiful. It is instead the result of a field that was not well designed or well constructed and that hasn't had the bypass surgery it desperately needs. A new generation of natural turf scientists have re-engineered what grass can do. Fast growing, soil and climate formulated grass seed is generations removed from what is on Mazzaro's field today. Some of us have learned from a natural turf expert that different grasses supported by new fertilization techniques and innovative maintenance protocols can support our athletic program. Several of our assumptions regarding natural turf fields also appear to be outdated. They include the number of hours a field needs to rest, faster and more robust growing grass seed, which requires two months rather than three seasons to grow, increased durability because of innovative maintenance techniques, and targeted irrigation, which ultimately saves water. If we install artificial turf at Mazaros Field, we won't gain much more playing time due to scheduling, daylight hours, and because Mazaros is our primary game field. Unless the district commits itself to installing lighting, the field is currently used about as much as it possibly can be. Artificial turf will not give us more hours, and artificial turf does not help us solve some of our other important problems, such as the poor playing conditions of Upper Dows Lane. I'd like to suggest that we instead invest our resources into building and maintaining the four natural turf fields that we own. In particular, I'd like to suggest that the district engage Jared Minnick as a consultant who can look at the plans for Eastfield and immediately evaluate Upper Dows Lane Field. I'd also like to see a bond that includes an option for a natural turf solution for all four fields, because I truly think that such a solution can serve our district's needs while being environmentally sound and sensitive to our school budget. Thank you.
